qs.q: A young adult presents with severe fatigue, generalized lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. Heterophile antibody test is negative. Cytomegalovirus serology is also negative. A blood PCR test confirms Epstein-Barr virus infection. How does EBV primarily infect host B lymphocytes?
o: Viral spike proteins bind to CD4 helper T cell membrane coreceptor sites.
Viral hemagglutinin binds directly to sialic acid residues on the surface.
Viral envelope protein gD interacts with herpesvirus entry mediator molecules.
Viral glycoprotein gp350 binds specifically to the CD21 receptor on B cells.
Viral surface antigens attach to complement receptor type one on cells.
qs.e: EBV infects B cells by viral gp350 binding to CD21 (complement receptor 2) on the host cell membrane.

qs.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with fever, malaise, and atypical lymphocytosis. Heterophile antibody test is positive. Which viral protein is primarily responsible for the transformation of B lymphocytes?
o: Latent membrane protein 1 signaling through NF-kB pathways
Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen 1 maintaining episomal replication
Viral interleukin-10 inhibiting T-cell activation and cytokines
B-cell receptor mimicry leading to constitutive cell activation
Viral thymidine kinase phosphorylating nucleotides for synthesis
qs.e: LMP1 mimics CD40 signaling, activating NF-kB and promoting B-cell proliferation and survival in EBV infection.

qs.q: Which specific host cell surface receptor is targeted by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) to infect human B lymphocytes?
qs.e: Epstein-Barr virus targets B lymphocytes by specifically binding to the CD21 cell surface receptor. CD155 serves as the host cell receptor for poliovirus.
qs.s: Medical Virology: Adenoviruses, Hemorrhagic Fever & Viral Receptors: MCQs

qs.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with a rapidly growing jaw mass. Biopsy demonstrates a proliferation of B-lymphocytes associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and a characteristic c-MYC translocation. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Burkitt's lymphoma is a proliferation of B-lymphocytes driven by a c-MYC translocation (t(8;14)) and is closely associated with Epstein-Barr virus. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma involve different tissues and viral associations.
qs.s: General Pathology Revision: Cell Injury, Inflammation & Adaptation: MCQs

qs.q: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from a uropathogen interacts directly with Toll-like receptor 4 on B lymphocytes. How is LPS classified based on this receptor engagement?
qs.e: LPS can directly stimulate B cells via pattern recognition receptors like TLR-4 without requiring T-helper cell assistance, making it a classic T-independent antigen. T-dependent antigens require helper T cell interaction for robust antibody production.

ai.title: B Lymphocytes
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: B lymphocytes are key antibody‑producing cells that can become malignant or depleted. Clinicians must recognise infections, autoimmune disease, and therapies that alter B‑cell numbers, and interpret limited tests in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: B lymphocytes are lymphoid cells that mature in bone marrow and produce antibodies. Diagnosis relies on peripheral blood counts, flow cytometry for CD19/CD20, and immunoglobulin levels.

t.b: Look for abnormal morphology such as hairy cells or large blasts; normal cells are small with dense chromatin
Detects CD19, CD20, CD5, CD10; abnormal patterns suggest lymphoma or leukemia
Low levels indicate hypogammaglobulinaemia; high levels may suggest hyper‑immunoglobulinaemia or monoclonal gammopathy

sections.p: Staging follows WHO for lymphomas and the Rai system for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. Severity is gauged by organ involvement and cytopenias.
b: Rai stage 0–IV for CLL; higher stages mean more lymphadenopathy and cytopenia

sections.p: In East Africa, infections (HIV, TB, malaria) and endemic parasitoses (schistosomiasis) drive B‑cell activation or depletion. Genetic immunodeficiencies and drug‑induced hypogammaglobulinaemia are also common.
b: HIV infection → B‑cell hyperplasia and dysregulation
TB or malaria → polyclonal B‑cell activation

sections.p: Patients may have recurrent infections, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. In malignancy, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, and bruising are typical.
Limited resources mean reliance on basic counts, smear, and simple serology. When unavailable, clinical judgement and empirical treatment guide care.
Rapidly enlarging nodes, unexplained fever, cytopenias, or organomegaly suggest aggressive lymphoma or leukemia and require urgent referral.
Treat underlying infection or malignancy, replace antibodies if deficient, and monitor counts. Avoid drugs that further deplete B cells unless indicated.

t.b: Can cause severe B‑cell loss and hypogammaglobulinaemia

sections.p: Regular CBCs, immunoglobulin checks, and infection surveillance. Vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza where feasible.
T‑cell lymphomas, myelodysplastic syndromes, and reactive hyperplasia can mimic B‑cell disorders.
Low B‑cell counts may be normal in elderly; high counts can be reactive. Smear artefacts can mimic blasts.
b: Atypical lymphocytes in malaria may be misread as blasts

faq.q: What is the most common cause of B‑cell depletion in East Africa?
faq.a: HIV infection is the leading cause, often compounded by malnutrition and concurrent infections.

faq.q: How do you differentiate reactive lymphadenitis from lymphoma when flow cytometry is unavailable?
faq.a: Look for constitutional symptoms, node size >3 cm, and cytopenias; reactive nodes are usually smaller and lack systemic signs.

faq.q: Why is rituximab avoided in active bacterial infections?
faq.a: It removes CD20+ B cells, impairing antibody production and increasing infection risk.

exam: A 32‑year‑old man with HIV presents with fever and night sweats. What is the next best investigation? — CBC with differential and flow cytometry to rule out lymphoma; start ART if not already on it.
A patient on rituximab develops recurrent sinopulmonary infections. What is the most likely explanation? — B‑cell depletion leading to hypogammaglobulinaemia; consider IVIG replacement.
A child has low IgG and recurrent otitis media. What is the first step in management? — Initiate immunoglobulin replacement and vaccinate against pneumococcus.
A 55‑year‑old woman has a 4‑cm cervical node and mild anemia. Which sign suggests lymphoma over reactive hyperplasia? — Presence of night sweats and cytopenia; node >3 cm.
A patient with CLL shows platelets 30×10^9/L. What complication should you monitor? — Risk of spontaneous bleeding and need for platelet transfusion.
A 28‑year‑old woman with splenomegaly has a peripheral smear showing large blasts. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; confirm with flow cytometry and cytogenetics.
